title: Masala Idli: Turn Leftover Idlis Into a Quick Spicy Snack
excerpt: This 15-minute tawa idli recipe uses pav bhaji masala and basic pantry staples to give day-old idlis a flavorful second life.
body:
• Masala idli is a 15-minute recipe that transforms leftover idlis into a crispy, spice-coated snack using pav bhaji masala, onions, and tomatoes
  • Refrigerating leftover idlis before cutting makes them firmer, preventing crumbling during cooking
  • The dish works as breakfast, an evening snack with chai, or a lunchbox addition — and helps reduce food waste
  • Variations include adding capsicum and curry leaves, or swapping pav bhaji masala for sambar powder depending on regional preference

Every South Indian household knows the idli surplus problem. You make a big batch of batter, steam more idlis than you can eat, and by the next morning the extras sit in the fridge looking a bit forlorn. Reheating them with sambar and chutney works, but masala idli — also called tawa idli — offers a far more exciting alternative.

The dish takes about 15 minutes, uses pantry staples, and produces a snack that bears almost no resemblance to the mild, spongy original. Chef Ranveer Brar's popular version relies on butter, pav bhaji masala, and a squeeze of lemon to create what he calls a "quick snack" that works any time of day. Other widely followed recipes from Tarla Dalal and Sanjeev Kapoor follow the same core technique with slight regional twists.

The Basic Method

Cut 5-6 leftover idlis into bite-sized cubes. If they have been refrigerated, they hold their shape better — a tip multiple recipe developers emphasize. Heat a tablespoon of oil or butter in a pan, then add your tempering: cumin seeds or mustard seeds, depending on whether you want a North or South Indian base.

Add finely chopped onions and sauté until translucent. Next come the tomatoes, green chillies, and the spice blend. Most recipes call for turmeric powder, red chilli powder, and the key ingredient — pav bhaji masala. Food site Slurrp recommends adding garam masala and a pinch of hing to round out the flavor profile. Cook until the tomatoes break down into a thick, coating consistency.

Add the idli cubes and toss gently. The goal is to coat every piece without breaking them apart. Cook for 2-3 minutes on medium heat, finish with lemon juice and chopped coriander, and serve hot.

Ingredients at a Glance

For two servings: 5-6 leftover idlis, 1 onion (chopped), 1 tomato (chopped), 2-3 green chillies, 1 teaspoon each of cumin seeds, ginger-garlic paste, red chilli powder, and coriander powder, half a teaspoon each of turmeric and garam masala, a pinch of hing, 1 teaspoon of pav bhaji masala, oil or butter for cooking, lemon juice, and coriander leaves for garnish.

Tarla Dalal's restaurant-style version uses butter and garlic paste as the base for a richer result. Ranveer Brar goes further, adding capsicum and a red chilli-garlic chutney for extra heat and a more elaborate street-food feel.

"Leftover idlis and some magic is all you need for this quick snack."

— Ranveer Brar, Chef

Variations and Tips

South Indian households often prefer a tempering of mustard seeds, curry leaves, and dried red chillies — closer to a traditional tadka — while the pav bhaji masala route leans distinctly North Indian. Both approaches work well. Food blog GyanhiGyan suggests substituting sambar masala for pav bhaji masala for a tangier, more traditional South Indian flavor.

A few practical tips from across recipes: use day-old idlis rather than fresh ones, as the slight dryness helps them absorb spices and hold their shape. Cut them into smaller cubes for better flavor distribution. And do not skip the lemon juice at the end — it lifts the entire dish.

A Staple for Diaspora Kitchens

For Indian families abroad, masala idli solves a common problem. Idli batter — whether homemade or store-bought from an Indian grocery — tends to come in large quantities. Making a full batch means leftovers are almost guaranteed. Rather than eating plain reheated idlis or letting them go to waste, masala idli turns them into something that works as a breakfast side, an after-school snack, or an evening accompaniment to chai.

The dish also travels well in lunchboxes, holding up better at room temperature than plain idlis. With prep time under five minutes and cooking time around ten, it fits easily into a weekday morning routine — a useful trick for any kitchen where idli batter is a regular fixture.
